title: A Star Ate a Planet—and Scientists Found the Proof in Its Belly!
summary:
Did you know stars can eat planets? It sounds like something from a sci-fi movie, but astronomers just found strong evidence that a star called TOI-5882 swallowed one of its own worlds. This star is about 1,300 light-years away and is a lot like our sun. So how did scientists figure out what happened? They looked at the star's chemical recipe and found a surprising ingredient: lots and lots of lithium.

Lithium is a light metal, and planets have way more of it than stars do. "You are what you eat, right?" joked Brooke Kotten, the scientist who led the study. "If a star eats a planet, it's going to take on a bunch of lithium." Think of it like this: if you eat a whole cake, someone could tell by the frosting on your face! The team used a method called spectroscopy—basically, they split the star's light into a rainbow to see what chemicals are in it. They found so much lithium that they think the swallowed planet was somewhere between the size of Earth and Neptune.

But why would a planet fall into its star? TOI-5882 hasn't puffed up into a giant yet, so it couldn't just reach out and grab the planet. The clue might be a brown dwarf orbiting the star. A brown dwarf is like a failed star—it's huge, more than 20 times heavier than Jupiter, but not big enough to shine like a real star. Its gravity might have kicked the planet out of its safe orbit and sent it plunging into the star.

This cosmic mystery is exciting because it could happen right here in our solar system. In about 5 billion years, our sun will swell into a red giant and might swallow Mercury, Venus, and maybe even Earth. By studying stars like TOI-5882, scientists can learn what signs to look for and how often planets get eaten. "We can't just watch the crime happen," Kotten said, "so we have to work with all the clues we're given to figure out whodunit." It's like being a space detective!
why_it_matters: By studying planet-eating stars, we can predict what might happen to our own solar system billions of years from now when the sun becomes a red giant—and it also helps us see how common this dramatic event is across the universe.

background_read: Stars are mostly made of hydrogen and helium, while rocky planets contain heavier elements like lithium. So if astronomers see an unusual amount of lithium in a star, it’s a strong hint that the star gulped down a planet. The star TOI-5882 (named after NASA’s TESS telescope that discovered it) is a sun-like star 1,300 light-years away.

Brown dwarfs are sometimes called 'failed stars' because they are not massive enough to start the nuclear fusion that makes normal stars shine. Their strong gravity can disturb planetary orbits, sometimes sending worlds plunging into their parent star.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists led by researcher Brooke Kotten
WHAT: Found evidence that the star TOI-5882 swallowed a planet—lots of lithium in its atmosphere gave it away
WHERE: The star system is about 1,300 light-years away from Earth
WHY: To understand how often stars eat their planets and to learn what signs to look for when it happens

perspectives.description: This is one of the best pieces of evidence yet that stars can swallow whole planets. Astronomers are excited because the lithium clue is strong and gives them a clear way to hunt for more planet-eating stars.

Some scientists warn that the extra lithium could come from other sources, like a star simply being born with more lithium. More observations are needed to be absolutely sure this was a planet dinner.

Since we can’t watch the act of a star eating a planet, astronomers have to work like detectives, collecting chemical fingerprints and orbital clues to piece the story together—just like solving a mystery without seeing the crime.
